vignette:
Arjun is 29 years old, a house painter by trade, married for three years to his wife, Priya. He is a lean, quiet man with steady hands-or at least he used to be. Before the robbery, he could spend eight hours on a ladder, cutting in ceilings with a two-inch brush, never once thinking about the street below. He worked mostly in the western suburbs of the city, where the homes were old and the clients patient. Priya would pack him a lunch of roti and spiced potatoes, and he'd listen to cricket matches on his phone while the paint dried.

The robbery happened on a Tuesday evening in November. He had finished a living room in a colonial bungalow and was walking to the bus stop, carrying his metal toolbox. The street was dim, the orange glow of streetlights flickering through the leaves of an old fig tree. Two men came from behind-he never saw their faces, only felt the hard pull of a hand on his collar and the cold circle of metal at his ribs. "Give it," one said. He dropped the toolbox. They kicked it open, took the money from his wallet, and then, for no reason he could understand, one of them struck him on the side of the head with the butt of the pistol. The sound was wet and dull, like a watermelon dropped on concrete. He fell to his knees. They ran. He stayed there for maybe ten minutes, curled on the pavement, his hands shaking so badly he could not dial his wife's number.

He does not remember calling Priya. He remembers her arrival, her hand on his arm, the way the emergency room smelled of bleach and antiseptic. The scan showed no fracture. The doctor said he was lucky. Arjun said nothing.

Since that night, the world has changed. It is not that he is afraid of the dark, exactly-it is that the dark now feels alive, as if it conceals the shape of a man waiting to press metal against his skin. He cannot walk to a bus stop alone. If he tries, his heart hammers so violently that his vision blurs and he has to lean against a wall. He has stopped taking jobs that require him to travel through the western suburbs. He tells his supervisor he has back pain. Instead, he works only in neighborhoods he knows intimately, or better still, on houses where the client is home and the front door stays locked.

His painting itself has suffered. He used to love the precision of a straight line, the clean edge where the wall meets the ceiling. Now his hands tremble when he holds a brush, especially if the ladder is tall. He has to pause, climb down, sit on the floor, and breathe. He thinks he hears footsteps below. He thinks he hears the clatter of his own toolbox hitting pavement, though it is always just the creak of an old house. He has started rushing-slapping paint on with rollers, leaving drips on the trim. The clients notice. One complained. He apologized, but inside he felt a hot shame that quickly turned into anger, and then the anger faded into a hollow blankness.

At home, he is irritable. Small things set him off: the click of a door latch, the sudden appearance of Priya behind him in the kitchen. He snapped at her last week for putting his clean brushes in a drawer without telling him. She cried. He did not know what to say. He still does not know what to say. He has not touched her in three months. He sleeps in a separate bed because at night his body goes rigid at every sound-a car passing, a distant siren. Sometimes he dreams of the gun barrel against his ribs, and he wakes up gasping, his fists clenched, the sheets soaked.

He has not told Priya all of this. He does not want to worry her. But she knows. Yesterday, she sat beside him on the sofa and said, very softly, "Arjun, your hands are never still." He looked down at his own fingers, twitching on his knees. He had not noticed.

Today, he is sitting on a plastic stool in an empty living room, waiting for the primer to dry. The house is quiet. The front door is double-locked. He has placed his toolbox beside him, not on the ground, because the sound of metal scraping concrete makes him nauseous. He stares at the wall. The line where the primer meets the raw plaster is uneven, but he cannot make himself stand up and fix it. He is thinking about November. He is thinking about how the street looked after the men left-the way the light fell on the brown leaves, the shattered plastic handle of his brush sticking out of the gutter. He does not know how to stop thinking about it. He only knows that the paint is drying, and that he needs to finish the job before dark, because after dark he cannot paint at all.
